The Story of King Manivrat

I bow to Lord Jinendra, worshipped by the world, to the supreme word of Jina, and to the gurus, and I write this story concerning the renunciation of worldly possessions.

In the land of Manivat stood a city also named Manivat. Its king was Manivrat, whose queen was Prithivimati. They had a son named Manichandra. Manivrat was learned, wise, and a fine warrior, and he governed his kingdom with great skill.

Through the ripening of merit, the king ruled well and lived happily. He had full faith in dharma, gave daily charity to the worthy, worshipped the Lord, and strove to do good for others. One day, as Queen Prithivimati was arranging the king's hair, she noticed a single white hair. She plucked it and placed it in the king's hand. The king saw that white hair as a messenger sent by death itself, and he became deeply detached from the world and its pleasures. He handed all the affairs of state to his son Manichandra and, after worshipping the Lord and giving gifts to supplicants, set out for the forest, where he took initiation as a monk and began practising austerities. Day by day he purified his soul and became absorbed in the contemplation of the Supreme.

As a wandering monk, Manivrat gave religious discourses in many lands. One day he came to the cremation ground outside Ujjain. At night he meditated among the funeral pyres, contemplating the Supreme in perfect peace. At that hour, a Kapalika — a practitioner of tantric rites — came to the cremation ground to perform a ritual to the goddess Betali. To build his fire-altar, he needed three corpses. He counted the monk as one and dragged two more bodies to the spot. He arranged the three heads into a fire-altar, placed a human skull on top, lit the fire, and began to cook an offering.

Suddenly the monk's hand rose involuntarily, and the skull on top fell off. The Kapalika, terrified, fled. But the monk remained immovable as Mount Meru, undisturbed by any fear. At dawn a passer-by saw the monk's condition and ran to tell a man named Jindatt. Jindatt rushed to the cremation ground and was overcome with grief at the sight. He brought the monk to his home and consulted a renowned physician for his treatment. Through devoted care, the monk recovered and continued his spiritual practice with renewed vigour.

The monk Manivrat continued his austerities, indifferent to pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour. He had already conquered all attachment when he saw that single white hair, and now nothing in the world could shake him. Ultimately he attained liberation.

This story teaches that the recognition of death's approach — even in a single white hair — can awaken the soul to renunciation. And when detachment is genuine, no force in the world, not even the horrors of a cremation ground at midnight, can disturb the peace of a soul established in dharma.
